author: Mike Shaughnessy Sun
title: MSHSL recognizes Gillen for success and service - NewsBreak
text:
By Mike Shaughnessy Sun ,
10 hours ago
Volleyball coach receives Hall of Fame induction
Coaching accolades are nothing new to Eagan High School's Kathy Gillen, but the one she received last weekend stands out.
Gillen, one of the state’s most successful high school volleyball coaches, was inducted into the Minnesota State High School League Hall of Fame on April 19 in St. Paul. She was one of 12 inductees in the 2026 class to receive the MSHSL’s highest honor. It’s not specifically a coaching award; inductees include athletes, officials, administrators and fine arts leaders.
In other words, it’s an award that recognizes recipients for being among the best at what they do, and thanks them for their service to Minnesota high school activities.
“It’s a great honor, and it’s humbling,” Gillen said. “I’ve had a handful of coaching awards, and those are a great honor too. But (the MSHSL Hall of Fame) is all sports and all fine arts activities. It’s going to be a lasting memory.”
Gillen’s Eagan teams won seven state volleyball championships in her 30 years as head coach. That’s the most of any coach in the large-school enrollment class. The Wildcats reached the state championship match seven years in a row from 2013-19. Her teams won 720 matches, 15 conference championships and 16 section championships. Four of her players were named Gatorade Minnesota Player of the Year, and Kennedi Orr won the Ms. Baden Volleyball Award in 2020.
All of it might not have happened if not for Gillen’s desire to teach math.
Becoming a math teacher and volleyball coach had been her goal since her high school days at Minneapolis Patrick Henry (now Minneapolis Camden). After graduating from the University of Minnesota she worked for a couple of years at Anoka High School. But the school wasn’t expected to have an opening in its math department for several more years, and a new high school going up in Dakota County caught her attention.
Gillen’s connections to Eagan? “Absolutely none,” she said. But the high school did have a math department opening, and it needed teachers with coaching backgrounds. Gillen was put in charge of the volleyball program. She was on board when Eagan High School opened for ninth-graders in the fall of 1989 (it expanded to grades 9-12 the following year).
“It was amazing,” Gillen said of being part of the staff that opened the high school. “I started with people like Dave Fritze (former Eagan football head coach) and Rob Graham (current Wildcats girls track and field head coach). All those people are still my friends today.
“I retired from full-time teaching in 2024 but I still sub because I love being at the school and seeing my friends.”
Eagan became one of the state’s strongest volleyball programs under Gillen’s direction. The Wildcats first got to the state tournament in 1996, starting a streak of eight consecutive state appearances that included four championships and one runner-up finish.
“I had a lot of mentors,” Gillen said. “Doug Smith was the coach at Columbia Heights (a state volleyball dynasty in the 1980s and ‘90s), and when I was in college I worked at his camps. After I was hired at Eagan I spent a lot of time talking with (former Apple Valley head coach) Walt Weaver about how to set up a program.”
Gillen said there were times she wondered if the Wildcats could get to the point where they could compete with the powerhouse programs Smith and Weaver ran. Before long, it was happening. In addition to the seven state championships, Eagan had five runner-up finishes.
Gillen and her three siblings played every sport available in their Minneapolis neighborhood, almost every day. She eventually gravitated to volleyball as her main sport but also was a state runner-up in badminton. Gillen was her high school’s Athena Award winner in 1982.
Once Gillen started coaching at Eagan, she derived satisfaction from knowing many of her top players were multi-sport athletes, like she was. The youth sports landscape has changed significantly, with volleyball a prime example. Between the high school and club seasons, the top players could be practicing and playing volleyball as much as 10 months a year, which leaves little time for other sports.
“The three-sport athletes, you don’t really see them in volleyball anymore,” she said. Playing two sports is tough enough, as Gillen experienced with her daughter McKenna Melville, an Eagan volleyball standout in the 2010s who also played softball.
“I’d drive her straight from the softball game to volleyball practice,” Gillen said. “She had a driver’s license, but it was easier if I drove so she could eat in the car.”
McKenna went on to star in volleyball at the University of Central Florida. By 2023 she was looking to start her career. She landed at her high school alma mater as – you guessed it – a math teacher. McKenna also was hired as the Wildcats’ volleyball head coach, with her mother becoming a varsity assistant.
Gillen said one of the things that made her happiest about her time at Eagan was the connection players had with the volleyball program even after they graduated. “We have four former players coaching in the program,” she said.
And one assistant coach with more than 700 career victories. Gillen said continuing to coach with the Wildcats is a year-to-year decision, but she will be back on the Eagan sideline in the fall and doesn’t sound like she’s in any hurry to leave.
“I coached a 12-and-under team last year,” she said. “I still love it.”
MSHSL Class of 2026
Joining Gillen in the 2026 MSHSL Hall of Fame class is Dave Wicker, a 1979 Burnsville High School graduate who served as an educator, coach and administrator in Minneapolis Public Schools for 41 years. He coached football, hockey, baseball and math team and eventually became the district’s assistant athletic director. He retired in 2023 and died March 5, 2026, after a 14-year battle with pancreatic cancer.
Remaining 2026 inductees and their induction categories: Randy Breuer, Paul Martin and Mary Jo Miller Hmielewski (athlete), Robin Ingram and Mark Kroulik (coach), Robert Crowe (official), Rich Matter (administrator), W. Rayford Johnson and Rebecca Meyer-Larson (fine arts), and Lou Nanne (contributor).
